itemRequests.readingquiz: Write two ORIGINAL passages from my notes, about 300 words each: one short story and one nonfiction article. passages.title: Biscuit
paragraphs: Mrs. Abara handed Kiran her spare key and a page of notes. "Biscuit is shy with new people, so don't take it personally," she said. At the bottom she had written: Dev will come Thursday to water the plants. Kiran had asked his parents for a pet for three years. Four days with Biscuit felt like a test, and he planned to get a perfect score.

On Monday morning the apartment was silent. Kiran filled the bowl and crouched by the couch. "Here, kitty, kitty!" He shook the food bag and tapped the bowl with a spoon, louder each time. He walked to school with his shoulders up near his ears.

That evening the bowl was empty, and the blanket on the armchair was warm and covered in orange hair. Kiran looked behind the mat. Nothing had spilled. At dinner his sister Tam said, "So she ate!" Kiran shook his head. "Dev must have come by and tossed it out. She won't touch anything I give her."

On Tuesday he tried harder. He waved a feather toy under the bed and sang to her. Two green eyes watched him from the dark, then slid away. "She misses Mrs. Abara too much to eat," he told Tam. "And she hates me." Tam shrugged. "Or you're loud."
On Wednesday evening Kiran had a math test to study for and no energy for singing. He sat on the floor against the couch, opened his notebook, and forgot to call her at all.

After a while, something warm leaned against his elbow. Biscuit sat beside him, staring at the page as if she were checking his work. Kiran did not reach for her. He kept writing, but slower. She stayed until he finished the last problem.

On Thursday, Dev was watering the plants when Mrs. Abara got home. She glanced at Kiran's notebook. "I used to teach math, you know." Kiran started to say, "She didn't eat at first," then looked at Dev and stopped. Biscuit was curled on the armchair, watching him. "Could I come over sometimes?" he asked. "I'd bring my homework."

passages.title: The Reeds of the North Lagoon
passages.source: Written for this quiz. Vessa Island, its people and its animals are invented.
paragraphs: Vessa Island has two shallow lagoons, North and South, with a strip of sand between them. Tall tolla reeds once grew thick along both shores. A long-legged gray bird called the drell nests only in thick reeds. At night it wades through the mud and eats kib snails.

In the winter of 1961, a storm flattened the reeds around the North Lagoon. The South Lagoon, behind higher dunes, lost only a few. With nowhere to nest, the North Lagoon's drells flew off. Some fishermen were glad. They believed drells ate young fish, though no one had ever seen one do it.

Everyone expected the reeds to come back in a year or two, as they had after smaller storms. They did not. Each spring, green shoots poked up from the mud, and each summer they were gone. Islanders blamed the salt the storm had washed in.

In 1968, a teacher named Hana Selk tested the North Lagoon's water and found it no saltier than the South's. Then she went out after dark with a lamp. The mud was crowded with kib snails, and they were eating the new shoots down to the roots. Without drells, almost nothing was eating the kibs.

The islanders first tried planting reeds by hand. The snails ate those too. So in 1971 Selk's students built wooden nesting platforms and hid them in the last reed clumps. Two pairs of drells moved in the next spring.

The change was slow. For five summers the shoots kept vanishing, and some islanders said the platforms were a waste of wood. By 1980, though, every platform was in use, the snails were thinner on the mud, and reeds stood again along the North Lagoon's shore.
The fishermen's catch did not drop when the drells came back. If anything, it rose. Young fish hide among reed stems.
Selk later wrote, "The storm knocked the reeds down. The missing birds kept them down."

questions.skill: infer a character's feelings or beliefs

prompt.A: In paragraph 1, how does Kiran feel about his four days with Biscuit?
prompt.B: In paragraph 4, what does Tam think the problem is?

A: nervous that Biscuit will not like him
sorry he agreed to watch someone else's cat
set on proving he can take care of a pet
sure the job will be easy and quick
B: Biscuit misses her owner too much.
Kiran is making too much noise.
Biscuit is shy with people she doesn't know.
The feather toy frightens Biscuit.

why.A: The four days "felt like a test, and he planned to get a perfect score" [1], after three years of asking for a pet. He shows no worry yet that Biscuit won't like him (that comes on Monday and Tuesday [3]-[4]); nothing shows he is sorry; he plans to work hard and never calls the job easy.
why.B: Tam answers Kiran's ideas with "Or you're loud" [4]. Missing Mrs. Abara is Kiran's idea [4], not Tam's; "shy with new people" is Mrs. Abara's warning [1]; the feather toy is only what Kiran waves [4].

prompt.A: In paragraph 5, why doesn't Kiran call Biscuit on Wednesday evening?
prompt.B: In paragraph 3, why does Kiran shake his head at dinner?

A: His mind is on the math test he has to study for.
He plans to ignore her so she will come to him.
Mrs. Abara's notes told him to leave her alone.
He has given up on ever winning Biscuit over.
B: He thinks Biscuit spilled most of it behind the mat.
He wants Tam to stop asking about Biscuit.
He believes someone else emptied Biscuit's bowl.
He thinks Biscuit ate only a few bites of it.

why.A: He has "a math test to study for and no energy for singing" and "forgot to call her" [5]. It is not a plan: he forgot. Mrs. Abara says Biscuit is shy [1], and the written note is about Dev's Thursday visit; nothing tells him to leave her alone. He has not given up: he forgot to call her, and on Thursday he asks to come back [7].
why.B: Tam says "So she ate!" and Kiran shakes his head: "Dev must have come by and tossed it out" [3]. He checked behind the mat and "Nothing had spilled" [3]; Tam is not nagging, she says one line; he does not think Biscuit ate any of it ("She won't touch anything I give her" [3]).

prompt.A: Part A: Near the end of the story, why does Kiran stop in the middle of a sentence?
prompt.B: Part A: In paragraph 7, why does Kiran offer to bring his homework when he visits?

A: He remembers he was told not to take Biscuit's shyness personally.
He sees Biscuit watching him and does not want to upset her.
He sees that Biscuit must have eaten the food herself.
He does not want to blame Dev for the food in front of him.
B: He hopes Biscuit will come sit by him again while he works.
He hopes Biscuit will let him pet her while he studies.
He thinks Biscuit likes being sung to while he works.
He thinks Biscuit is lonely without Mrs. Abara.

why.A: Two steps: on Monday Kiran said Dev "must have come by and tossed it out" [3], but the note says Dev comes Thursday [1], and Dev is only now there [7]. Seeing Dev, Kiran sees nobody threw the food out, so Biscuit ate it. He was told not to take her shyness personally [1], but his half-sentence is about the food ("She didn't eat at first" [7]), not her shyness; Biscuit is calm on the armchair [7], and he looks at Dev, not at her, when he stops; Dev could not have tossed the food on Monday, so there is nothing to blame him for.
why.B: Two steps: on Wednesday Biscuit sat beside him while he did math and "stayed until he finished the last problem" [6]; on Thursday he looks at Biscuit watching him and then offers to bring homework [7], so he connects her coming near with him sitting and working. He "did not reach for her" [6], so petting is not what drew her; he had "no energy for singing" on Wednesday [5], and singing made her slide away [4]; missing Mrs. Abara was his wrong Tuesday idea [4].

prompt.A: Part B: Which quotation from the story BEST supports the answer to Part A?
prompt.B: Part B: Which line from the story BEST supports your Part A answer?

A: "Biscuit is shy with new people, so don't take it personally," [1]
"Dev will come Thursday to water the plants." [1]
"On Monday, Dev's watering can sat by the empty bowl." [3]
"Biscuit was curled on the armchair, watching him." [7]
B: "When he reached out, she rubbed her head on his hand." [6]
"He sang softly to her as he did his math." [5]
"She misses Mrs. Abara too much to eat," [4]
"She stayed until he finished the last problem." [6]

why.A: Key: the note shows Dev was not coming until Thursday [1], so he could not have tossed the food on Monday, and Biscuit ate it. The shy line [1] backs "told not to take her shyness personally"; the armchair line [7] backs "does not want to upset her." "On Monday, Dev's watering can sat by the empty bowl" is unmatched (backs "blame Dev"): the passage contradicts it, since Dev comes Thursday [1] and Kiran only guesses "Dev must have come by"; the real line in [3] is "That evening the bowl was empty, and the blanket on the armchair was warm and covered in orange hair."
why.B: Key: Biscuit stayed beside him until his homework was done [6], so she comes near when he sits and works. "She misses Mrs. Abara too much to eat" [4] is real and backs "lonely without Mrs. Abara." "When he reached out, she rubbed her head on his hand" is unmatched (backs "let him pet her"): the passage contradicts it; the real line in [6] is "Kiran did not reach for her." "He sang softly to her as he did his math" is unmatched (backs "likes being sung to"): the real line in [5] says he had "no energy for singing" and "forgot to call her at all."

prompt.A: On Tuesday, what does Kiran try, and how does Biscuit respond? Quote the sentence that shows how she responds and give its paragraph number.
prompt.B: On Monday morning, what does Kiran do to get Biscuit to come out? Quote one sentence that shows it and give its paragraph number.

answer.A: He waves a feather toy and sings; she looks at him and then moves away: "Two green eyes watched him from the dark, then slid away." [4]
answer.B: He calls her and makes more and more noise with the food: "He shook the food bag and tapped the bowl with a spoon, louder each time." [2]

A: feather toy and singing; she watches, then goes away, quoting "Two green eyes watched him from the dark, then slid away." [4]
he tries harder with a toy and a song; she watches him, then slides away, with the [4] sentence
B: shakes the food bag and taps the bowl louder each time, quoting the [2] sentence
calls "Here, kitty, kitty!" and makes noise, quoting a [2] sentence

why.A: Full credit: the toy or the singing, her watching and then slipping away, and the [4] sentence. "She hides" or "she ignores him" with no line from [4] earns at most half credit.
why.B: Full credit: calling or the bag and bowl noise, plus a [2] sentence. "He calls her" with no line or detail from [2] earns at most half credit.

sections.heading: Questions 6-12: "The Reeds of the North Lagoon"

questions.skill: find a detail in the text

prompt.A: According to the article, when did the first drells move onto the platforms?
prompt.B: According to the article, who built the nesting platforms?

A: the same summer the platforms were built
five summers after the platforms were built
in 1980, once the reeds stood again
the spring after the platforms were built
B: the fishermen of the North Lagoon
islanders from the South Lagoon
Hana Selk's students
Hana Selk and the fishermen

why.A: The platforms were built in 1971, and "Two pairs of drells moved in the next spring" [5]. Five summers is how long the shoots kept vanishing [6]; 1980 is when every platform was in use [6]; nothing says drells moved in the summer of building.
why.B: "Selk's students built wooden nesting platforms" [5]. The fishermen are only mentioned as glad the drells left [2] and in the catch [7]; Selk is never said to have built them herself; South Lagoon islanders are not mentioned.

questions.skill: infer a cause the text does not spell out

prompt.A: Why did the drells most likely stay away from the North Lagoon for years after the storm?
prompt.B: Why did the South Lagoon most likely lose only a few reeds in the 1961 storm?

A: The fishermen kept chasing them away.
Too few thick reeds were left for nesting.
Salt from the storm had killed the snails they ate.
There was too little food left for them to eat.
B: Its higher dunes kept the worst of the storm away.
Its drells kept the hungry snails off the young shoots.
Its water was much less salty than the North Lagoon's.
Its reeds grew farther from the open sea.

why.A: Drells nest only in thick reeds [1]; the storm flattened the North's reeds [2], the new shoots were gone each summer [3], and only the last reed clumps were left [5]. Drells came back once platforms were hidden in those clumps [5]. No one chased them (they flew off with nowhere to nest [2]); the kibs crowded the mud [4], so they were not killed; food was not short, since the mud was crowded with kibs [4], which drells eat [1].
why.B: The South Lagoon is "behind higher dunes" and "lost only a few" [2]: the dunes sheltered it from the storm. The snails ate shoots after the storm, not during it [3]-[4]; Selk found the North no saltier than the South [4]; the article never says where the open sea is.

prompt.A: Based on the article, why did the North Lagoon's reeds stay away after 1961, when they had come back after smaller storms?
prompt.B: The first drells moved onto the platforms in 1972, but the new shoots kept vanishing for years afterward. Based on the article, what most likely explains the delay?

A: This storm drove off the birds the new shoots depended on.
This storm left salt in the water that never washed out.
This storm buried the roots under sand from the dunes.
This storm drove off the fish that ate the snails.
B: Salt from the 1961 storm was still in the water.
Two pairs of drells were too few for all the kibs.
The new drells ate young fish, not kib snails.
The reed roots needed years to heal from the kibs.

why.A: Two steps: after 1961 the drells flew off [2]; without drells almost nothing ate the kibs, and the kibs ate the new shoots [4]; so shoots that came up each spring were gone each summer [3]. Selk found the water no saltier than the South's [4]; shoots came up every spring [3], so the roots were not buried; no fish are said to eat snails, and without drells "almost nothing was eating the kibs" [4].
why.B: Two steps: only two pairs moved in at first [5]; by 1980 every platform was in use and the snails were thinner on the mud [6]; so it took more drells to thin out the kibs. Selk found the water no saltier than the South's [4]; drells eat kib snails [1] and no one had seen one eat fish [2]; shoots came up every spring [3], so the roots were alive, and the shoots vanished because kibs ate them [4].

questions.skill: infer why the author includes a detail

prompt.A: Part A: Why does the author tell about the islanders planting reeds by hand?
prompt.B: Part A: What does the article suggest about the belief that drells ate young fish?

A: to show that new plants could not last while the snails went uneaten
to show that salt left by the storm still killed young plants
to show that planting by hand worked for a while
to show that the islanders did not want the drells back
B: It was proved true by fishermen in 1960.
It was true, though the harm to the fish was small.
It led the fishermen to drive the drells away.
It was only a guess, with nothing to back it up.

why.A: Two steps: the hand-planted reeds were eaten too [5], and without drells almost nothing ate the kibs [4]; so planting could not work until something ate the snails, which is why the platforms came next [5]. Selk found the water no saltier than the South's [4]; the planted reeds were eaten, not standing [5]; nothing says the islanders as a whole wanted the drells gone (only some fishermen were glad [2]), and they built platforms to bring them back [5].
why.B: Two steps: "no one had ever seen" a drell eat young fish [2], and when the drells came back the catch did not drop and if anything rose [7]. So nothing backed the belief. Nothing shows it was proved (no one saw it [2]); nothing shows any harm to fish (the catch rose [7]); the drells flew off because they had nowhere to nest [2], not because fishermen drove them away.

prompt.A: Part B: Which quotation from the article BEST supports the answer to Part A?
prompt.B: Part B: Which line from the article BEST supports your Part A answer?

A: "Islanders blamed the salt the storm had washed in." [3]
"By summer the planted reeds stood tall along the shore." [5]
"Some fishermen were glad." [2]
"The snails ate those too." [5]
B: "They believed drells ate young fish, though no one had ever seen one do it." [2]
"In 1960, fishermen counted dozens of drells eating young fish." [1]
"The fishermen's catch did not drop when the drells came back." [7]
"The fishermen chased the last drells off with nets." [2]

why.A: Key: the planted reeds were eaten by the snails [5], so new plants could not last while the snails went uneaten. The salt line [3] backs "salt left by the storm still killed young plants"; "Some fishermen were glad" [2] backs "the islanders did not want the drells back." "By summer the planted reeds stood tall along the shore" is unmatched (backs "planting by hand worked for a while"): the passage contradicts it; the real line in [5] is "The snails ate those too," and shoots kept vanishing for five summers [6].
why.B: Key: the belief had no sighting behind it [2]. "The fishermen's catch did not drop" [7] is real and backs "true, though the harm to the fish was small." "In 1960, fishermen counted dozens of drells eating young fish" is unmatched (backs "proved true"): the passage contradicts it; the real line in [1] is "At night it wades through the mud and eats kib snails," and [2] says no one had ever seen a drell eat a young fish. "The fishermen chased the last drells off with nets" is unmatched (backs "drive the drells away"): the real line in [2] is "With nowhere to nest, the North Lagoon's drells flew off."

questions.skill: infer why the author includes a detail

prompt.A: Why does the author say Selk went out after dark?
prompt.B: Why does the article say the platforms were hidden in the last reed clumps?

A: to show she was searching for the drells that had left
to show the shoots were being eaten at night
to show that her water test had to be done at night
to show she did not want the fishermen to see her
B: because a storm like the one in 1961 might flatten them
because snails could not climb into thick reeds
because drells will nest only where reeds grow thick
because hunting birds might spot them

why.A: After dark, with a lamp, Selk saw the mud crowded with kib snails eating the new shoots down to the roots [4]; drells also feed at night [1]. Nothing says she was looking for drells; she tested the water before going out [4]; the fishermen are not in [4], and nothing says she hid from anyone.
why.B: The drell "nests only in thick reeds" [1], and the last reed clumps [5] were the only reeds left standing to hide the platforms in. Nothing says the clumps sheltered the platforms from storms or that snails cannot climb reeds (they ate the shoots [4]); hunting birds are never mentioned.

questions.skill: word meaning from context, with evidence

prompt.A: What does "thinner" mean as it is used in paragraph 6? Quote a sentence from an earlier paragraph that helps show the meaning, and give its paragraph number.
prompt.B: What does "in use" mean as it is used in paragraph 6? Give one detail from another paragraph that shows it happening, and give the paragraph number.

answer.A: Fewer and more spread out, not crowded: "The mud was crowded with kib snails, and they were eating the new shoots down to the roots." [4]
answer.B: Being used for nests; drells were nesting on the platforms: "Two pairs of drells moved in the next spring." [5]

A: fewer / not as many snails, quoting the [4] sentence about the mud crowded with kib snails
less crowded, spread out, with "The mud was crowded with kib snails" [4]
B: had drells nesting on them; two pairs of drells moved in [5]
being used by drells as nests, with the [5] detail about drells moving in

why.A: Full credit: a meaning like "fewer / less crowded" plus the [4] sentence about the crowded mud. "Skinnier" is the everyday sense and does not fit. A meaning with no line from the passage earns at most half credit.
why.B: Full credit: a meaning like "had drells nesting on them" plus the [5] detail of the two pairs moving in. "Used by people" or "being fixed" does not fit. A meaning with no detail from the passage earns at most half credit.

sections.heading: CONSTRUCTED RESPONSE (4 points)
sections.directions: Write your answer on the lines.

prompt.A: How does Kiran change from the beginning of "Biscuit" to the end? Use RACE: R - Restate the question. A - Answer it. C - Cite two pieces of evidence with [paragraph numbers]. E - Explain how each piece of evidence proves your answer.
prompt.B: How does the way Kiran treats Biscuit change from Monday to Wednesday evening? Use RACE: R - Restate the question. A - Answer it. C - Cite two pieces of evidence with [paragraph numbers]. E - Explain how each piece of evidence proves your answer.

answer.A: Kiran changes from trying hard and loudly to win Biscuit over to being calm and patient. At first he calls and taps the bowl "louder each time" [2]. Later he "did not reach for her" [6], and he asks to come back [7].
answer.B: Kiran goes from chasing Biscuit with noise to leaving her alone and letting her come to him. He taps the bowl "louder each time" [2] and sings to her [4]; on Wednesday he "did not reach for her" and kept writing [6].

why.A: Score with the RACE CHECKLIST. Strong evidence: [2] or [4] for the start; [5], [6] or [7] for the end. The Explain row needs how each quote shows the change.
why.B: Score with the RACE CHECKLIST. Strong evidence: [2] or [4] for Monday and Tuesday; [5] or [6] for Wednesday evening ([7] is Thursday, outside the question). The Explain row needs how each quote shows the change.

rubric.title: RACE CHECKLIST

criteria.name: Restate

I answered, but part of my answer is unclear.
My answer only partly fits the question.
I did not answer the question.

levels: I used two quotes, each with a [paragraph number].
I used two quotes, but one has no [paragraph number].
I did not use any quotes.

criteria.name: Explain
levels: I explained how each quote proves my answer.
I said the quotes prove it but not how.
I did not explain my quotes.

facts.notes: Adapted brief: p2 ('Trouble in the East Valley') is invented on purpose (owner's decision), so it was checked for INTERNAL consistency only, not against an outside reference. findings.where: passage p2, all paragraphs (internal consistency)
findings.what: No paragraph contradicts another. Dates and order: 1961 storm [2]; shoots fail each spring and summer [3]; 1968 test [4]; hand planting, then 1971 platforms, first pairs the next spring [5]; five slow summers, then by 1980 the reeds are back [6]. Places: North = flattened, drells gone, snails crowded, platforms, regrowth; South = higher dunes, lost only a few, used as Selk's salt comparison. Who did what: the storm flattened the reeds; the drells flew off; some fishermen were glad; islanders blamed salt; Selk tested and found the snails; islanders planted by hand; Selk's students built the platforms.
